name: Naltrexone/Bupropion (Contrave)

lead: Contrave is a daily extended-release tablet combining naltrexone and bupropion. It is approved to help adults with obesity or overweight lose weight alongside diet and exercise.
Trials report weight loss over placebo, but network meta-analyses place it below semaglutide and tirzepatide.

paras: Bupropion raises dopamine and noradrenaline and activates appetite-suppressing neurons in the hypothalamus, while naltrexone blocks the opioid feedback that would otherwise damp that effect, so the pair reduce appetite and cravings.

Reviews note constipation in about 20% of users of centrally acting weight drugs; nausea, headache and insomnia are also reported. Bupropion carries warnings about suicidal thoughts and seizure risk and can raise blood pressure. Prescription-only.

lead: Naltrexone/bupropion, sold as Contrave (Mysimba in some markets), is a fixed-dose oral combination of an opioid-receptor antagonist and an antidepressant and smoking-cessation drug, approved for chronic weight management in adults with obesity or overweight alongside diet and exercise [1][2][3]. It is one of the centrally acting weight-loss drugs reviewed alongside phentermine-topiramate [1].

Phase 3 trials, including COR-I, COR-II and COR-BMOD, compared the sustained-release combination with placebo over about 56 weeks [4][5][6]. Network meta-analyses rank it as producing smaller average weight loss than semaglutide or tirzepatide [7][8]. A JAMA review lists constipation among adverse effects of centrally acting drugs in about 20% of patients [1].
The combination has also been studied for binge-eating disorder and methamphetamine use disorder [9][10][11]. No community discussion specific to the drug appears in the sources reviewed.

paras: Clinical guidelines and reviews include naltrexone/bupropion among the approved medications for obesity, to be used with lifestyle intervention [1][2][3][12]. Researchers have also tested it for binge-eating disorder, loss-of-control eating after bariatric surgery and stimulant use disorders [10][13][14][15][9].
Weight loss is its appearance-relevant effect. Weight outcomes are modest compared with newer incretin drugs [7][8].

COR-I, a multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, studied naltrexone plus bupropion in overweight and obese adults [4]. COR-II examined weight and risk factors [5]. The 56-week COR-BMOD trial randomized 793 participants to placebo or naltrexone SR 32 mg/day with bupropion SR 360 mg/day, both with intensive behavior modification [6].

Meta-analyses of obesity drugs report that naltrexone/bupropion lowers weight versus placebo, with smaller effects than semaglutide and tirzepatide [16][7][8]. Other trials: a 2022 trial in binge-eating disorder [10][11][13], a New England Journal of Medicine trial in methamphetamine use disorder using injectable naltrexone plus oral bupropion [9], and registered studies after bariatric surgery, on weight maintenance and on food addiction [17][18][19][14][15].

Reviews report constipation in about 20% of patients taking centrally acting weight-loss drugs, with other effects varying by drug [1]. Nausea, headache and insomnia are commonly listed for this combination in product information, and bupropion labelling carries a warning about suicidal thoughts in young people; individual product labels give the full list of warnings, including blood pressure and seizure risk.

Bupropion inhibits reuptake of dopamine and noradrenaline and stimulates hypothalamic pro-opiomelanocortin neurons; naltrexone blocks the opioid-mediated feedback that dampens that effect, so the two together are described as reducing appetite and food reward [1][20].

Registered phase 4 studies examine metabolic and behavioral mechanisms of Contrave in obesity, and use in breast cancer survivors and in diabetes remission programs [21][22][23]. A review of psychostimulant withdrawal management also covers the combination [24].
